claims.text: Formal workplace groups are deliberately created through the organisation to carry out an assigned purpose. Management identifies a task, allocates members and responsibilities and establishes reporting. Informal groups develop through repeated interaction, friendship or shared interests outside the official structure. Working near one another can create contact; trust and common interests can then sustain the group. A person can belong to a department and a friendship group at the same time. The distinction concerns how the group forms and its relationship to official organisation, not whether it is large or useful. An informal group is not automatically a trade union or an outside association.

claims.text: Fictional Omi Workshop appoints a safety team. Separately, workers who travel together become friends and regularly help one another. The appointed safety team is formal. The friendship group develops informally through shared contact, even if some friends also belong to the safety team.

claims.text: Formal groups coordinate assigned work, share specialist knowledge and clarify responsibility. Informal groups can provide belonging, support newcomers and spread practical information quickly. Both can help cooperation, but neither is automatically beneficial. A formal team can suffer unclear roles or poor coordination. Informal group norms can support quality or encourage resistance, exclusion and rumours. Managers should understand relationships, communicate accurately and address harmful behaviour rather than assume all friendships disrupt work. Group influence matters because staff can follow trusted peers as well as formal instructions. Assess what the group actually does and whether it supports legitimate work objectives.

claims.text: Fictional Nela Foods’ friendship group helps new staff find equipment and understand routines. Its official dispatch team coordinates order completion. Informal support can improve confidence and cooperation while the formal team clarifies the delivery task. If friends exclude a newcomer, the same informal influence can instead harm work; management should address exclusion without abolishing helpful relationships.

claims.text: A formal group is deliberately established within the organisation for an assigned work purpose, with defined membership or responsibilities. Examples include a department, committee or project team. Clear roles and shared knowledge can support the task, but creating a named group does not ensure effective cooperation.

claims.text: An informal group arises through relationships or common interests outside the official organisational structure. It can give members belonging, practical support and a quick route for information. Its norms can also spread rumours or exclude others. Informal does not mean unimportant, unlawful or necessarily opposed to management.
